# The politics of integrating health systems and public programs: a review of political headwinds, tailwinds, and policy maker recommendations

**Authors:** Nolan M Kavanagh; Anil Menon; Adrianna McIntyre

**Affiliations:** 1 Interfaculty Initiative in Health Policy, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, United States | 2 Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, United States | 3 Department of Political Science, University of California, Merced, Merced, CA, United States | 4 Department of Health Policy and Management, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, United States

## Abstract

Amidst low trust in public institutions, policy makers and scholars have proposed using the health system to help rebuild trust in other institutions. One potential mechanism to do so is linking the health system with public programs, e.g. simple referrals, shared financing, or delivering social services via the health system. While other reviews have examined the technical aspects of such linkages, few have examined the political calculus involved. We conducted a narrative review of the academic and grey literature on the relationship between health and trust in public institutions, as well as political considerations when integrating health systems and social programs, including the attitudes, concerns, and constraints of beneficiaries, stakeholders (e.g. service providers), and political actors. For beneficiaries, attitudes about the health system are associated with attitudes about public institutions, and linking the health system to less popular public programs has been shown to increase engagement in the latter. However, unsuccessful handoffs and administratively burdensome social programs can alienate beneficiaries. Stakeholders are often eager to partner in linkages but can become frustrated by redundant roles and uncoordinated financing. For political actors, embedding social services in the health system may be logistically easier than maintaining standalone programs, but it may also result in weaker long-term public support. Thus, linking health systems and public programs can produce mutual “co-benefits” when done well. At the same time, policy makers must consider the political trade-offs inherent in the linkage. Future research should directly test whether these linkages causally impact broader social outcomes, such as political trust.

## Introduction

Public institutions are facing a crisis of trust [1, 2]. Across the world, a growing share of the population is wary of the services provided by their governments and, in turn, is disengaging from public institutions, supporting anti-establishment political movements that promise to restructure those systems, and even rejecting the democratic process [3, 4].

Amidst low institutional trust, many people place more faith in their health systems than in their governments [4]. Nearly everyone engages with the health system at some point, and many do so regularly. Even more than the broader health system, people are especially trusting of their individual nurses, doctors, and other clinicians [5, 6]. Yet despite having more faith in the health system than the government, sizable proportions of populations still identify health and the health system as the responsibility of government [7].

Consequently, scholars and policy makers have proposed using the health system as a conduit to promote participation in public institutions and restore trust in them [8]. One potential mechanism for doing so is “linking” health systems and public programs together [9–11]. We consider a broad spectrum of linkages to be relevant—including streamlined applications for standalone health and social programs, using the health system to refer patients to programs for which they are eligible, and even financing and delivering social services via the health system. Previous reviews have examined the technical aspects of integrating health and social services [9–12], including ways to measure the success of integration [13].

In this narrative review, we focus on the politics of linking health systems and public programs. That is, what are the potential political consequences of leveraging the health system to bolster trust and engagement in public programs? This includes the considerations underlying the decision to maintain freestanding programs or to fully integrate those services into the health system. We start by discussing the relationship between health, trust in the health system, and trust in broader public institutions. Then, we examine several aspects of linkages and their political nuances: (i) public support and the experiences of users, (ii) the roles of stakeholders and other institutional challenges, such as funding, and (iii) policy feedback as relevant to political actors considering implementing linkages.

Policy makers of diverse contexts can benefit from considering the political headwinds and tailwinds of linking health systems and public programs. Those in strong welfare states can use the insights to assess whether the health system would be a politically useful partner in bolstering existing programs. Meanwhile, policy makers planning to build up social services can use the insights to inform the choice between creating standalone programs and using the health system as a foundation for delivering them.

When linkages are done well, institutions can flourish together. When done poorly, linkages can produce frustrating experiences for beneficiaries and stakeholders. In doing so, they may exacerbate mistrust in public institutions and even damage the reputation of the health system, the very institution whose high regard was initially leveraged.

## Methods

This article is structured as a narrative review of the politics of integrating public programs and social services into the health system, with a special focus on the potential consequences for public trust. Our goal is to highlight discussions spanning multiple literatures and make novel connections between them. Given that few studies have directly taken on the question in a directly measured and consistent fashion, we chose a narrative review, rather than a systematic review. This way, we can explore the underlying theoretical framework and shed light on the tensions that require additional research or consideration.

To identify relevant articles, we searched Google Scholar and PubMed for works published up until 1 August 2025. Our search terms included “health system and public program integration,” “health system and social services,” “the politics of health-social service linkages,” “health and political or public trust,” “health systems and politics,” and iterations on those themes. We considered original research and reviews published in scholarly journals, academic working papers, and works in select “grey” outlets, e.g. polls or policy briefs by non-academic organizations. We took care to consider the contributions of several disciplines, including public health, medicine, social work, and political science. We did not impose a strict date range for relevance, although all selected works were published after 2000.

All candidate publications were screened for relevance by the first author and included after confirmation by the second and third authors. Then, we summarized the key findings for each topic outlined in the introduction. Given journal constraints on citation counts, when multiple identified articles were relevant to a topic, we selected a typical representative to include. Consequently, our citations are neither exhaustive nor fully inclusive; rather, they were selected to represent several active literatures.

Lastly, to help motivate why scholars and policy makers have proposed using the health system as a conduit to boost public trust, we included one original analysis that compares attitudes about several institutions. We used data from waves 2 to 11 of the European Social Survey, spanning 2004 to 2024 and 39 polities, since few other surveys interrogate attitudes about governmental institutions alongside the health system [14]. Respondents were asked to rate a variety of institutions on 0–10 scales from “extremely bad,” “extremely dissatisfied,” or “no trust at all” (0) to “extremely good,” “extremely satisfied,” or “complete trust” (10). We present unadjusted means with 95% confidence intervals using post-stratification and population weights.

## Results

### Overview of included publications

We selected 40 publications that directly bore on the political considerations of integrating public programs into the health system. The academic articles spanned several disciplines, including medicine and public health [6, 8, 12, 13, 15–23], social work [9–11, 24–28], political science [1, 3, 29–36], and other social sciences [2, 7, 37–40], although many eluded clear categorization. We directly cited one public poll [5] and one policy brief [4], although additional contributions by non-academic organizations are represented in other citations. The works were diverse in approach, including causal evaluations with well-identified counterfactuals, descriptive studies with cross-sectional surveys, and qualitative explorations. They provided international perspectives, with the bulk representing North America (especially the USA and Canada) [2, 4–10, 12, 13, 16–22, 24, 28, 31–34, 36–40] and Europe [1, 3, 4, 6–8, 11, 13–16, 23, 25–29, 34, 35], plus select works in Asia [7, 13, 14, 16, 30], Australia and New Zealand [7, 13, 16, 28], Africa [13, 16, 30], and South America [30]. All works were published after 2000, although a few used data from before 2000.

### The political connections between health, health systems, and public institutions

A large body of work has documented the complex connections between people’s health and their broader social, economic, and political conditions [15]. Our environment shapes our health, and our health, in turn, affects our ability to maintain employment, stay socially active, and engage in civic life. These bidirectional relationships mean that decisions about the health system do not exist in isolation from other policies or political decisions.

People in poor health are expected to interact with public institutions more than their healthier neighbors. Not only do they require more health care, but they also tend to have higher rates of extra-clinical needs, such as poor housing, food insecurity, unemployment, and limited transportation, all of which may lead them to engage with public programs [12]. More touch points mean more opportunities to build—or damage—their trust.

To that end, there is a close association between health, experiences with institutions meant to support health, and trust in those institutions. People with better health are more likely to view the health system positively [29]. Perhaps because the health system provides meaningful benefits during vulnerable times, people tend to have more positive attitudes about it than other public institutions. As an illustration of the health system’s high regard, we compared Europeans’ evaluations of the health system against those of a variety of other institutions from 2004 to 2024 (Fig. 1). Although the scales vary depending on the institution being evaluated, assessments of the health system were generally more favorable than those of parliament, the legal system, and even democracy. On the flip side, many patients encounter stigma in health care settings due to their health conditions or sociodemographic characteristics [16]. Similarly, beneficiaries of public programs have reported demeaning experiences while trying to navigate complex enrollment processes and service delivery [38]. As such, worse health and negative experiences when accessing services are associated with more negative attitudes about the offending institutions [29].

*Figure 1.: Europeans’ attitudes about the health system and other public institutions. We used data from waves 2 to 11 (years 2004 to 2024) of the European Social Survey across the following 39 polities: Albania, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Kosovo, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Montenegro, Netherlands, North Macedonia, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Russia, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, UK, and Ukraine (although not all polities participated in all waves of the survey). Response options ranged from 0 to 10 using the indicated scales. For each outcome, we report the unadjusted mean and 95% confidence interval. Estimates were weighted by the survey’s post-stratification and population weights. Note that the confidence intervals are sufficiently narrow that they are difficult to visualize. N = 390,787.*

Importantly, the attitudinal impacts of negative health care experiences may not remain limited to the offending institutions but generalize to others. For many people in ill health, their primary experience of government and its efforts to serve the public is through the health system. Majorities or near-majorities of international populations—including in countries with highly privatized health systems—identify health as a responsibility of the government [7]. Consequently, unpleasant experiences while seeking health care might engender negative assessments about the government or reinforce pre-existing sentiments.

Associational evidence provides some support for this attitudinal generalization. In an analysis spanning 38 countries, worse assessments of the health system predicted lower trust in government [30]. Using data from 19 European countries, another study found that people in poor health reported not only lower satisfaction with the health system but also lower political trust more broadly [29]. Political trust was moderated by the extent of social welfare provided by the state—respondents in the poorest health in nations with robust welfare states reported greater political trust than those in the best health in other nations. This attitudinal generalization may even manifest in political behaviors: Poor health has been linked to support for extremist parties that promise to restructure “broken” systems [3]. That said, it is difficult to find rigorous causal evidence for this hypothesis [4].

Even so, policy makers and researchers have wondered whether the relatively high trust placed in the health system could allow it to serve as a conduit for improving attitudes about other public institutions [8]. Put differently, could the health system lend some of its goodwill to rescue other institutions that are suffering a crisis of confidence? One mechanism for achieving this goal could be linkages between the two, either by directing patients from the health system to freestanding but less popular public programs or by directly delivering social services within hospitals, clinics, and other health system sites.

At first glance, a transfer of trust may be possible. People who present to hospitals are often demographically distinct from those already connected to other civic processes [17], and people in poor health tend to be less trusting of their governments and political actors [4, 29]. As such, integrating services presents an opportunity to civically engage a difficult-to-reach group. We discuss the political nuances of these linkages next.

### Beneficiary experiences of linkages between health systems and public programs

Policy makers seek (or should seek) to optimize the experiences and trust of people who will actually use the social services linked to the health system. Linkages ranging in complexity from simple referrals to the full delivery of public benefits via the health system have successfully increased participation in social services [9–12]. However, the nature of beneficiaries’ experiences could have political consequences, both desirable and not.

Few works have directly solicited beneficiaries’ attitudes about health-social service linkages, yet they emphasize the importance of positive experiences. In a survey of patients and caregivers at several US health centers, the majority agreed it was “appropriate” for the health system to screen for extra-clinical needs [22]. In interviews, several respondents praised previously successful handoffs to additional services. However, others—especially those who had experienced unsuccessful handoffs—expressed skepticism that the health system was equipped to address their extra-clinical needs and were pessimistic that future handoffs would succeed, if they occurred at all [22]. Other interviewees conveyed privacy concerns, i.e. that disclosing extra-clinical needs to the health system could lead to bias and discrimination by their clinicians. A related dimension is digital data privacy; in a survey of Swedish patients, those with lower faith in the health system’s ability to protect digital data were less willing for that data to be used for non-clinical purposes, such as education (although respondents were not specifically asked about linkages to social services) [23]. Whatever the reason, 40%–60% of patients who reported extra-clinical needs across several studies declined to participate in additional services [12]. Consequently, an attempted linkage alone is likely insufficient to transfer positive attitudes from the health system to other programs and, when done poorly, could do the opposite.

A useful case study for understanding the political opportunities and perils of linking health systems and public programs is the interplay between three US programs for low-income individuals: Medicaid, a public health insurance program; the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), a food assistance program that provides beneficiaries credits for purchasing food items; and the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), which provides food assistance as well as breastfeeding support.

In 2014, a change in federal law allowed states to optionally expand their Medicaid programs—and, with it, access to the health system—to large portions of low-income Americans. Using quasi-experimental study designs, researchers have shown that states that expanded Medicaid also saw increased uptake of SNAP and WIC [39]. This uptake was partly attributable to streamlined eligibility criteria and applications, as well as shared outreach efforts between the programs [18]. This shared uptake is notable since the public has more favorable views of Medicaid than other public assistance programs, which suffer substantial stigma in the USA [31, 32]. By linking less popular and less utilized programs to a well-funded and well-publicized one, the engagement in all of them increased.

However, depending on the nature of the programs being linked, there may be downside political risks to tasking the health system with connecting individuals to other social programs. Social programs vary in the extent to which they are accessible and laden with administrative burdens, or learning, compliance, and psychological costs that beneficiaries encounter while seeking services [40]. SNAP has complex documentation obligations, including work requirements for many enrollees, as well as frequent eligibility recertifications. In one study comparing administrative burdens across social programs in the USA, SNAP case workers reported pressure to meet deadlines while managing overwhelming caseloads, and beneficiaries described feeling stigmatized by their interactions with the often-inaccessible case workers who managed their eligibility and benefits [38]. By contrast, workers in WIC reported that the program facilitates sustained personal interactions with participants, and clients rarely reported stigmatizing or demeaning experiences [38].

When public program design produces an experience of interacting with the government that is onerous or stigmatizing, there is a risk that using the health system as a conduit to those programs could backfire. Scholars have documented how negative interactions with means-tested programs can alienate individuals from government, eroding trust and decreasing political participation [34]. In this way, linking to difficult-to-navigate social programs is unlikely to bolster trust in them. One might even worry that the frustrations and stigma that beneficiaries experience in public programs could, in some cases, rebound onto the referring health care entity and inadvertently damage its own reputation.

A dilemma here is that the programs characterized by the most severe administrative burdens are also the ones that are plausibly most ripe to embed in the health system—to wit, there is no need to ask the health system to act as a conduit if a public program is well-understood, easily navigated, and leaves beneficiaries feeling empowered. Policy efforts to coordinate enrollment or outreach across sectors might consider going beyond simply reallocating administrative tasks to new stakeholders (whose perspectives are also relevant, which we consider in the next section). They also ought to consider strategies to address and reduce the underlying administrative burdens and potential for stigmatization.

Unfortunately, we are not aware of any evaluations that have causally demonstrated that linkages between the health system and public programs can improve institutional trust. Although many studies have used patient- and provider-centered outcomes to measure the success of linkages, these measures tend to focus on narrower aspects of the experience, such as satisfaction with care or perceived involvement in decision-making [13]. Evaluations rarely, if ever, consider broader social outcomes, such as political trust.

### How do we best engage stakeholders in linkages?

In addition to beneficiaries, it is important to consider the perspectives of other stakeholders. These include clinicians, social workers, civil servants, and workers in non-governmental organizations, all of whom must coordinate to provide reliable, integrated services to populations. As one sign of political opportunity, stakeholders are often eager to support linkages and believe that the unique contributions of each stakeholder can complement one another [19, 24]. However, political challenges can and do arise in attempts at coordination that can hinder the delivery of social services and damage stakeholders’ support.

One challenge is reconciling the similar yet distinct interests of different stakeholders. While all stakeholders are committed to providing high-quality care and services, values like autonomy can create frictions. For example, non-governmental organizations that partner in delivering social services can hesitate to relinquish their independence to the degree necessary to successfully integrate their services with other entities [25, 26]. Organizations also worry about redundancy in service provision with other organizations [19], which may require governments or health systems to choose “winners” amongst them.

Even when interests are aligned in health-social service integration, there can be conflicts of authority. One study in Norway interviewed frontline professionals and managers of health and community organizations about the cooperative management of patients with complex health and social needs [27]. Clinicians and social workers frequently disagreed on basic definitions like “ready for discharge,” as some patients would be medically “ready” but had not yet been prepared for their outpatient social needs. Consequently, it was non-obvious who should have the final say in when and to where patients were discharged.

This conflict of authority also applies to public perceptions of responsibility. When scholars and policy makers call on the health system to help solve broader social problems, often implicit is that clinicians—as the public face of the health system—are responsible for providing solutions. However, medical training rarely prepares clinicians for social service provision, while non-clinical stakeholders like social workers, public health workers, civil servants, and workers in non-governmental organizations are typically better prepared for this role. By tasking the health system with solving problems beyond its capacity, the health system stands to lose public trust if the problems persist. To balance these concerns, decision makers must ensure that public perceptions of responsibility include non-clinical stakeholders—and direct sufficient resources to them to make meaningful dents in the problems.

### Who is financially responsible?

Another important political challenge in linking health and social services is financing. Health systems and public programs are typically financed via separate streams that are difficult to integrate [28]. One study interviewed civil servants, especially government budget and finance directors, in several urban jurisdictions in the USA about health and social service integration [20]. A major challenge they noted is that patients’ needs often span several domains, including health, housing, food, etc., but that the public agencies responsible for each have strict funding restrictions that make the provision of comprehensive services challenging. Reconciling them can require legislative action at the national level, yet failing to reconcile them can leave patients with disastrous gaps in service delivery.

In cases where funding has been successfully integrated between health and social services and the impacts were evaluated, the evidence for improved health, spending, and other outcomes is muted [28]. A review of 38 financing schemes from eight mainly high-income countries, including several randomized trials, found that integrated financing by itself did not consistently affect health, costs of care, or utilization [28]. Relevant for our purposes, there were generally positive effects on user experiences of care. Even so, financial integration is merely one aspect of linkages that may determine “success.” Previous reviews have examined other technical aspects of integration, and we defer that discussion here [9–11].

### The risks of submerging social services in the health system for political actors

For political actors, one of the attractions of health-social service linkages is that they “submerge” potentially unpopular programs in the health system’s complex structure [33, 36]. Many members of the public oppose expanding government benefits to “undeserving” populations [37]. Placing these benefits in the health system with targeted outreach to eligible patients can make them less visible to voters than standalone programs with broad public outreach—and, therefore, subject to less opposition. Additionally, modifications to existing health infrastructure may be logistically easier to implement, requiring mere incremental regulatory tweaks, rather than the passage of de novo social programs through the full legislative process and the buildup of administrative capacity.

However, for the same reason that these maneuvers are politically appetizing, they are also more easily undone. This ease of undoing includes the reversal of regulatory tweaks by later political administrations, whereas legislative actions may be more durable. It also includes weaker bases of public support through policy feedback mechanisms [34].

Policy feedback is the concept that policies or programs can generate their own constituencies that politically support those programs into the future [34]. Such feedback is more common when programs provide meaningfully large benefits, target visible or easily identifiable groups of people (with universal programs being especially powerful), and are otherwise politically salient [34]. Submerging social services within the health system fails to produce a single, visible program around which the public can rally support. It also makes it less clear whom the public should politically reward for successes. Moreover, people in poor health—who would tend to use services within the health system—are less likely to turn out to vote and participate in political organizations than healthier folks, reducing the incentives for politicians to throw legislative capital behind such initiatives [17, 35].

Consequently, political actors might consider the trade-offs inherent in using the health system to supplement or replace services that would otherwise exist as visible, standalone programs. Although the work of building and maintaining a beloved social program is hard, the public often rewards political actors who do so—for decades [34].

## Discussion

Amidst low trust in public institutions, scholars and policy makers have taken an interest in using the health system to help rebuild that trust [8]. As we have described, the public maintains positive attitudes about health care professionals and the health system, and there is the potential for mutual political “co-benefits” in linking the health system with public programs [4]. However, there are also potential pitfalls, including the risk of negative beneficiary experiences in burdensome linkages, alienated stakeholders, uncoordinated financing, and weakened political incentives. We summarize these points in Table 1.

*Table 1. Summary of the political opportunities and perils of linking public programs to the health system, with recommendations for policy makers*

| Actor | Political opportunities | Political perils | Recommendations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Beneficiaries | Enhanced services, improved health and well-being, and potentially greater institutional trust | Burdensome navigation of linkages and stigma that may damage trust in the health system and government | Ensure smooth linkages that maximize access, meet beneficiaries’ needs, and promote respect |
| Clinicians, social workers, civil servants, and other stakeholders | Enthusiasm and aligned missions to deliver high-quality services | Misaligned values (e.g. autonomy), redundant service provision, and uncoordinated financing streams | Set clear expectations for roles, coordinate financing, and appropriately attribute responsibility |
| Policy makers and political actors | Easier provision of services that may be politically contentious to deliver via standalone programs | Submerged services that are less visible than standalone programs and generate weaker political “wins” | Ensure that successful linkages are politically salient to maximize their long-term political viability |

This review leads to several recommendations for policy makers considering whether to use the health system to bolster trust in public institutions (Table 1). For one, they should seriously consider the political trade-offs between linking standalone programs and truly embedding social services within the health system. While the latter has several conveniences, it may suffer from longer-term political weaknesses. Regardless of the nature of the linkages, policy makers should ensure that successes are politically salient not only to maximize the policies’ political viability but also to realize gains in public trust. Second, policy makers should ensure that navigating linkages is smooth and minimally burdensome for beneficiaries, lest they risk low uptake or, worse, damaging trust in both the health system and public programs. Third, policy makers should set clear expectations and roles for stakeholders, including clinicians, social workers, and workers in non-governmental organizations, with explicit funding streams, clear responsibilities, and mechanisms for evaluation.

An important limitation of this review is the lack of high-quality causal evidence, which reflects the limited evidentiary base. It is challenging to identify a causal relationship between health, institutional experiences, and political trust, given that health and its associated experiences are rarely exogenous. Although the associations are consistently strong, the exact nature of the relationships remains unclear. Moreover, it is yet to be tested whether integrating health and social services has a meaningful impact on institutional trust. Evaluations of linkages tend to measure proximal outcomes, such as satisfaction with services, rather than downstream political ones [13]. Future research should directly take on the question of which political “co-benefits” are provided by linkages and under what circumstances.

To the broader question of this review, should the health system be responsible for providing social services and, more generally, helping rebuild trust in public institutions? Some experts have raised the alarm about over-relying on the health system to fix social ills that are more so the purview of government [21]. Part of the objection is logistical: Health systems are overburdened, they are often inefficient providers of social services, services can become tied to a site’s limited catchment area, and so on. But as we have reviewed here, policy makers must also consider the political trade-offs inherent in using the health system to address a crisis of trust that began outside its walls. If done poorly, such linkages could further weaken trust in all participating institutions.

## Ethical statement

This study did not require institutional review board approval because it used publicly available, de-identified data.

## Data availability

All replication materials for the original data analysis using the European Social Survey are available at the Harvard Dataverse (https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/T0AU50).

- Amidst low trust in public institutions, policy makers and scholars have proposed linking public programs to the health system to leverage the relatively high esteem of the health system to bolster trust and engagement in other institutions.

- There are several potential political “co-benefits” to linking health systems and public programs, such as reaching patients via the health system who are otherwise civically disconnected and typically have lower trust and participation in government.

- However, there are also several potential political perils, such as poor beneficiary experiences with administrative complexities, stakeholder frustrations, and limited policy feedback mechanisms to reward political actors and protect linkages long-term.

- Policy makers should consider the political trade-offs involved in using the health system to bolster trust in public programs and ensure that linkages are thoughtfully designed to promote positive experiences for both beneficiaries and stakeholders.
